work_order.understanding:
#51 landed three tests that pin the page h1 to its .page-title stylesheet rule, so AC-2 ('the page title renders at 22.4px with no top margin') is machine-checkable. This ticket closes the eight holes in that guard, all of which I re-verified on main.

Six come from the review of #54 and two from QA on it, and after deduplication they are five defects, not eight:

1. The class-attribute extractor is /\bclass="([^"]*)"/. A word boundary matches inside data-class=, so <h1 data-class="page-title"> satisfies it: the suite is green while no class attribute exists in the markup and the heading falls back to the UA default. The issue proposes /<h1\s[^>]*\bclass="([^"]*)"/ as the fix. That does not fix it — [^>]* consumes the 'data-' and \b is a boundary between '-' and 'c', so it matches the same false shape. I ran both against the string; both return 'page-title'. The fix is to anchor on whitespace: /\sclass="([^"]*)"/, which returns undefined for data-class= and still matches the class in either attribute order.

2. The pinning test finds its anchor with .find() over the file's own lines, and its own line 971 contains the anchor literal, so deleting the real call site at line 135 makes .find() return the search line. The test still fails, but on the wrong assertion.

3. The class-to-markup and class-to-stylesheet links are held by two independent literals, and three statements in #51's work order (approach §3, out_of_scope[2], risks[0]) say a coordinated rename of page-title passes on purpose. It does not: renaming both sides to .pageHeading gives 2 failures. The reviewer offers two fixes and says not to do both. The 'correct the work order' half of that choice is not available here — #51 is merged and its work-order.json is a historical artifact no ticket can edit — so the code half is the only one that can be taken, and I take it: read the class off the rendered h1 and resolve the stylesheet rule dynamically, keeping the three literal declarations.

4. A later, higher-specificity h1 rule overrides .page-title with the suite fully green. Appending '#main h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; line-height: 1.6; margin-top: 24px; }' leaves every .page-title declaration intact, node --test reports 271 pass / 0 fail, and the heading then computes 38.4px in the browser. The existing test pins declarations as text, which cannot see the cascade, and no test in the suite reads a computed style. This is the only finding here that is a live hole in shipped behaviour rather than a hole in a guard.

5. The fileURLToPath import at line 7 exists only to wrap import.meta.url for readFileSync, twenty lines before a test that uses the URL form directly.

6. The test file's comment declares a deliberate exception to .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md ('class names are styling hooks, not assertions'), but that memory file cannot be edited by any ticket and does not mention the exception. Not fixable in code; named in out_of_scope with the note the Librarian needs.
work_order.root_cause:
Every finding is one of two root causes, and neither is in the production code — src/web/pages.js:56 and src/web/styles.css:137 are correct as shipped and this ticket changes neither.

The first is that the guard pins strings instead of the thing the string stands for. The class name was hard-coded at both ends of a link that is supposed to be held by a check, the search for the production call site matched the search itself, and the class attribute was located by a pattern loose enough to match a different attribute. Each is a literal standing in for a fact.

The second is that a declaration is not a rendering. The stylesheet test asserts three declarations exist on .page-title; CSS decides what a browser applies by cascade, so a rule that outranks it — higher specificity, or equal and later, including inside a @media block — leaves every assertion satisfied and the heading wrong. Nothing in the suite can observe the result, because a computed style needs a browser and this suite is node:test with no DOM.

The three declaration assertions (margin: 0, font-size: 1.4rem, line-height: 1.25) stay literal and unchanged — AC-5 is about the declarations, not the name, and pinning them is what keeps the coordinated rename cheap. The rule-name assertion message must name the class the h1 actually carries so a one-sided rename says which end moved. Rename the test to 'the rule the page h1 carries still holds the declarations the page title depends on'. §5 — Add a cascade test after it, and this is the real work. 'nothing outranks the page title rule for the typography the h1 depends on'. It reads src/web/styles.css, strips comments, and for each of font-size, line-height and the margin-top bucket (margin, margin-top, margin-block, margin-block-start) works out which rule the browser would actually apply to

and asserts the winner is the class rule. - Candidate selection. A selector branch can reach the page h1 if it contains h1 as a type token anywhere, or its last compound carries the page-title class, or its last compound is *, html or body (those reach the h1 by inheritance, and being generous here can only produce a failure, never a pass). Split comma lists into branches first; evaluate each. A branch that cannot reach the h1 is skipped without being parsed, so an exotic selector elsewhere in the file — .checklist li:not(.x) — is ignored and never breaks the suite. Skip at-rules and keyframe selectors (a selector starting with @, or 0% / 100% / from / to). - Specificity. Count #id (a), .class, [attr] and single-colon pseudo-classes (b), and bare type names (c) over the branch; * counts as nothing. Rules in a @media or @supports block are evaluated as ordinary candidates — a responsive override of the h1's font-size is a real override at narrow widths and the failure message must name the at-rule condition so the reader knows when it bites. - A candidate outranks the class rule when (a, b, c) is greater, or equal and the candidate is declared later in the file. For each outranking declaration of a property in scope, fail with a message naming the branch, the property and the class rule's winning value. Note that a later '* { font-size: 2.4rem }' does NOT fail: the class still wins at (0,1,0) and the h1 is unaffected, so failing there would be a false alarm. The existing reset at line 25 and the body typography at line 31 must both pass, which is the check that the resolver is not simply flagging everything. - Unsupported syntax throws. Supported: id, class, attribute, single-colon pseudo-class, type, *, comma lists, descendant and '>' combinators. Anything else — a pseudo-element, '+', '~', a functional pseudo-class such as :not(…) — throws an Error naming the offending selector, so an unparseable stylesheet fails the suite loudly instead of passing for the wrong reason. Only candidate branches are parsed, so this cannot fire on unrelated CSS. I wrote and ran this resolver against the real stylesheet before planning: clean tree green, QA's appended '#main h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; line-height: 1.6; margin-top: 24px; }' red on all three properties, the same rule inside '@media (max-width: 900px)' red, the same rule moved above .page-title red on specificity, a coordinated rename to .pageHeading green, a later '* { font-size: 2.4rem }' green, and '.checklist li:not(.x)' ignored without throwing. Follow that shape; the differences between it and your implementation are where the bug would be. Pin the resolver itself in the same test — it is a test helper making a claim about CSS, and an unpinned one is a new false pass: '#main h1' beats '.page-title', '.a.b' beats '.a', '*' beats nothing, a '>' combinator is not a type name, and ':not(' throws rather than parsing to zero. §6 — The call-site pinning test at line 969. Delete the 'import { fileURLToPath }' dependency per §1, build the needle from parts so the search line cannot match itself — 'the h1 carries the page-title' + ' hook' — and add one assertion that the needle occurs exactly once in the file: assert.equal(source.split('\n').filter((line) => line.includes(needle)).length, 1, 'the anchor is found exactly once'). That is what turns the finding from diagnosability into a real pin: with the needle un-splittable, deleting the production call site makes .find() return undefined and the existing assert.ok(callSite, 'the 25-shell h1 assertion is still in this file') fires on itself, which is the message the reader needs. §7 — Rewrite the comment at lines 977-980. It currently says the assertion is a deliberate exception to .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md, which is true, and the file that would record it cannot be edited by this pipeline. Say that in the comment: the exception is deliberate, the class name is the single hook that reaches the stylesheet rule, and .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md is owned by the Librarian and does not yet record the exception — so the next agent who reads that file should not read this test as a convention violation or delete it as redundant. After all of this the literal 'page-title' appears in the test file only inside the H1_HOOK matcher comment and the shipped-markup sample strings at lines 146-152, which pin the behavioural testid, not the class.

risks: The cascade resolver is a test helper that makes a claim about CSS, and an unpinned one is a new false-pass surface — the same failure mode this ticket was filed for. It is mitigated by throwing on unsupported syntax rather than guessing, and by pinning its own specificity cases, but a selector form it reads wrongly (a pseudo-class counted as a type, a compound mis-split) would be a silent hole. Treat any change to its vocabulary as a change to a guard.

A legitimate responsive override of the page title inside a @media block now fails the suite. That is intended — a narrow-width font-size on the h1 makes AC-1 false at that width — but it means a future responsive-typography ticket has to change this guard deliberately rather than discover it as a surprise failure. The failure message names the at-rule condition so the reader knows when it bites.

The guard fails on declarations, not on the rendered heading. A stylesheet whose cascade this resolver mis-models could still render differently from what the test claims. The browser acceptance criteria AC-1 and AC-6 are the only thing in this pipeline that observes the real result, and they are checked once per run rather than per commit.

validated_work_order.understanding:
The previous attempt got the hole right and the fix's shape wrong. All six acceptance criteria pass, the shipped app is untouched, and the four defects QA filed are all in the 500 lines the previous work order itself specified inside test/web/pages.test.js. Nothing here is a defect in production code: src/web/pages.js:57 and src/web/styles.css:137 are correct as shipped and this change touches neither.

What attempt 1 got wrong, plainly: it built the cascade guard as a thing that pattern-matches selector TEXT, and then asserted — in approach §5 and in the comment above mayReachPageTitle — that doing so could only produce a failure, never a false pass. That guarantee is false, and each of the four bugs is a way it is false.

1. BUG-1 is that guarantee inverted. mayReachPageTitle recognises the class only in dot form: the compound must start with a bare h1, or be *, html or body, or contain '.page-title'. '[data-testid="page-title"]' starts with '[', carries no h1 token and contains no dot, so the pre-filter returns false and the branch is never parsed — while the browser matches that selector against the shipped h1 exactly, at (0,1,0), later in the file, and applies it. The enumerating filter is the wrong shape: it asks 'does this selector look like the ones I thought of', and the question has to be 'can this selector match this element'.

2. BUG-3 is the mirror, and it is the plan's own specification. Approach §5 said a branch reaches the h1 if 'its last compound carries the page-title class, or its last compound is *, html or body', and parseSelector implements exactly that. Deciding from the last compound alone means any '<something> h1' claims to be the page h1, so '.page-title h1' — which targets a descendant h1 of the page title, of which there are none — is reported as an override with a message stating as fact a change that does not happen. The plan's risks[0] predicted this exact hole ('a compound mis-split would be a silent hole') and shipped it.

3. BUG-4 is the plan's own specification too. §5 said 'Split comma lists into branches first' and the implementation splits on /\s*?>\s*|\s+/, with no regard for brackets or quotes, so the space inside h1[data-x="a b"] cuts one compound in two and the guard throws. The plan made throwing the contract for unmodelled CSS, which is a defensible instinct, but it then applied the same throw to CSS the guard's own comment lists as supported vocabulary.

4. BUG-2 is a gap the plan designed in. The plan kept the declaration test pinning three literals through .exec — which takes the FIRST rule carrying the class — and separately had the cascade test take the LAST declaration of each property as its winner. Two tests, two different rules, and nothing joining them: a class that appears twice with different values satisfies both while the browser renders 38.4px. The plan's own risk note said the resolver's vocabulary 'has to be pinned by its own cases or it becomes a new false-pass surface'; its cases pinned the resolver, never the pair of tests.

So the diagnosis is rewritten. The guard does not fail because CSS is hard to model. It fails because it decides 'is this the page h1' from the spelling of a selector instead of from the element the markup actually renders, and because the value the cascade finally settles on was never compared with the value the page title depends on. Both are structural, and both are fixed by changing what the guard reasons about, not by adding spellings to the list it recognises.
validated_work_order.root_cause:
One cause behind BUG-1 and BUG-3, and a second behind BUG-2 and BUG-4.

The first is that the guard was given a class NAME and asked to recognise it inside selector text. mayReachPageTitle is a whitelist of spellings ('.page-title' with a dot, 'h1' as a whole compound) and parseSelector sets matchesPageTitle from the last compound alone (lastCarriesClass || lastIsH1 || lastIsUniversal), so both halves of the question 'can this selector match the page h1' are answered by string shape rather than by the element. A whitelist under-approximates: any spelling it did not think of is a false pass (BUG-1), and a last-compound test over-approximates: any branch ending in h1 is claimed to be the page h1 (BUG-3). The plan's claim that being generous in the pre-filter 'can only produce a failure or a throw, never a false pass' is what the implementation violated in both directions at once.

The second is that the two halves of the guard were pinned independently. The compound splitter is a plain whitespace regex with no bracket or quote awareness, so a space inside a quoted attribute value cuts a selector in half and the guard throws on vocabulary it claims to support (BUG-4) — a direct consequence of approach §5's 'split comma lists into branches first'. And the class rule's winning declaration is never compared with the declarations the page title depends on: the declaration test reads the first rule carrying the class with .exec while the cascade test takes the last declaration of the property as its winner, so a stylesheet that declares .page-title twice with different values satisfies both and renders at 38.4px (BUG-2).
validated_work_order.approach:
Test-only, confined to test/web/pages.test.js, and a rewrite of the matching layer rather than an extension of it. The production files are correct and are not touched.

The principle: the guard must stop asking 'does this selector look like the page h1' and start asking 'can this selector match the page h1', with the h1 resolved once from the rendered markup. The question then has exactly one safe answer in each direction — a PROOF of non-match is allowed, nothing else is.

§1 — Resolve the page h1 into an element, once. Add a helper that scans the rendered HTML's tags, maintains an open-element stack (skipping comments and void elements: area base br col embed hr img input link meta source track wbr), and returns the element carrying data-testid="page-title" together with its ancestor chain, root-first. Each element is { tag, attrs, classes } with attrs a lowercased name → value map. This is the hook .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md already calls stable, so the guard's notion of the page h1 stops depending on the styling class. pageTitleClass() stays and is now read off the returned element, so the two ends of the class-to-rule link keep moving together under a coordinated rename.

§2 — One quote- and bracket-aware splitter. Replace both uses of /\s*>\s*|\s+/ with a scanner that walks the branch character by character, tracking a bracket/paren depth and a quote state, and only breaks on whitespace or '>' at depth 0 outside quotes. Both the matcher and the specificity function must use this one splitter, or they can drift on the same selector. This is what closes BUG-4: 'h1[data-x="a b"]' is one compound, and because the shipped h1 carries no data-x the rule is then provably unable to match it.

§3 — Match a compound against an element, and the branch against the chain. compoundMatches(compound, element) walks the simple selectors with a #id, .class, [attr] (with = ~= ^= $= *= |=), type and * forms, returning true or false. matchCompounds then requires the rightmost compound to match the h1 itself and each compound to its left to match an element to the left of the one it qualifies — a descendant anywhere in the chain, a child immediately before it for '>'. This is what closes BUG-3: '.page-title h1' needs an ancestor carrying .page-title, and the chain is html < body < main#main < h1.page-title, so the rule is provably a no-op and the guard stays quiet.

§4 — Make the reachability answer one-directional, and delete mayReachPageTitle. branchReaches(branch, chain) returns false ONLY on a proof of non-match, and true in every other case, including every case the vocabulary cannot decide:
  - a pseudo-class is undecidable from markup, so strip it and decide on the base. Because :not(), :is(), :has() and pseudo-classes in general only remove or re-target and never add, a base that matches nothing PROVES the original matches nothing; a base that matches leaves the answer true (may match), which reports the rule rather than guessing. So 'h1:hover' and 'h1:not(.x)' are reported and '.checklist li:not(.x)' is skipped — both without a throw.
  - a pseudo-element styles a generated box, never the element itself, so a branch containing '::' is false.
  - '+' and '~' need sibling information the chain does not carry. Decide the rightmost compound first, because that much is provable with no tree ('h1 + p' is false, since the page h1 is not a p); anything that gets past it returns true.
This removes the whitelist that caused BUG-1 and the throw that caused BUG-4. It is strictly the direction the plan claimed for itself: over-approximating reachability can only produce a reported override — a failure — never a false pass. The throw-on-unsupported contract is not carried over, and the four assert.throws cases in 'the cascade resolver agrees with CSS on specificity' are re-specified against the new guarantee rather than deleted: a selector that may reach the h1 is reported, one that provably cannot is skipped, and both directions are asserted.

§5 — Close the cross-test gap (BUG-2). Add one exported constant naming the declaration each guarded group must finally be settled by — { 'font-size': 'font-size: 1.4rem', 'line-height': 'line-height: 1.25', 'margin-top': 'margin: 0' } — and have BOTH tests read it: the declaration test asserts the class rule contains each of those, and the cascade test compares the class rule's WINNING declaration for that group against it, ignoring any !important. A stylesheet declaring .page-title twice now reports: the second rule's 2.4rem is what the cascade keeps, so the page h1's font-size would be 2.4rem instead of font-size: 1.4rem. Keep the three existing literal assertions in the declaration test — the values must stay visible in the test, not only in a table.

§6 — Keep what was already right. The !important model (importance outranks specificity, asymmetrically, and an ancestor's !important is still only an inherited value), the winner-selection rule across several class rules, the @media/@supports lifting with the condition named in the message, the shorthand-to-group reporting, the message wording that names the selector and the property, and the three pinning tests for the class extractor, the call site and the class-name exception. Change nothing about how a rule is turned into declarations or how specificity is compared; only what 'this selector can match the h1' means.

§7 — Pin the new guard. Every case above needs a test: the four QA repros verbatim, the element-derived chain, the one-directional property in both directions, and the coordinated-rename green. Keep the existing ~25 guard cases; re-express only the four that asserted the throw.

risks: The rewrite replaces a guard that works on the shapes it was written for with one that works on the shapes the markup actually contains. Every case the previous attempt pinned must be re-run against the new matcher, and the ones that assert the throw have to be re-expressed rather than copied; a case that cannot be re-expressed against the one-directional contract is a case whose guarantee the new design dropped, and that is a stop, not something to quietly delete.

Over-approximating reachability is deliberately the noisy direction: a rule that MAY match the page h1 and declares one of the three guarded properties is reported. A future stylesheet using a functional pseudo-class on the h1, or a sibling combinator, will therefore be reported rather than skipped. That is the correct direction — a reported override is a failure, never a false pass — but it is a behaviour change from attempt 1, which threw on those instead.

The element chain is read from the rendered markup of one route, so the guard reasons about '/' and assumes the other four shells put the h1 in the same place. That is already pinned by AC-6 and by the 25-shell test, and layout() is the only producer of the h1, so the assumption holds today. If a future page ever nests the h1 differently, this guard's world-model is wrong for that page and the failure is a missed report rather than a false alarm.

The specificity arithmetic is unchanged but now shares its splitter with the matcher, so a selector shape that tokenises differently between the two would mis-order the cascade. Keeping both on one splitter is the mitigation, and a case that pins the two against the same selector list is worth adding if the implementer has budget.

This is still a test helper that makes a claim about CSS, which is the same failure mode the ticket was filed for. It is mitigated by the one-directional contract — there is no shape that yields a silent pass, only shapes that yield a false failure — but a change to the guard's vocabulary is a change to a guard and belongs in its own commit with its own pinned cases.

The class-name assertion remains a deliberate exception to .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md, which is owned by the Librarian and still does not record it. The new guard leans on the data-testid hook rather than the class, which reduces how much rests on the exception, but the pin itself is still there and the Librarian's note is still owed on #51.

Appending '[data-testid="page-title"] { font-size: 2.4rem; }' → 51 pass / 0 fail in test/web/pages.test.js (BUG-1). '[class~="page-title"] { font-size: 2.4rem; }' → 51 pass / 0 fail (BUG-1). A second '.page-title { font-size: 2.4rem; }' → 51 pass / 0 fail (BUG-2). '.page-title h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; }' → 50 pass / 1 fail with the message 'the selector ".page-title h1" sets font-size: 2.4rem and outranks .page-title at (0,1,1)' on a tree the browser renders unchanged (BUG-3). 'h1[data-x="a b"] { font-size: 2.4rem; }' → 50 pass / 1 fail with the thrown "the cascade guard cannot read the selector 'h1[data-x=\"a b\"]': the token '[data-x=\"a'" (BUG-4).

The guard is right about the shapes it reaches and wrong about the ones its pre-filter never hands it.

The replacement matching layer is validated, not proposed. I wrote it standalone against the real rendered page (renderPage('/') with a fresh database) and ran it over 41 selector shapes: it returns the browser's answer on all of them. Reach: '#main h1', '[data-testid="page-title"]', '[class~="page-title"]', '.page-title', 'main .page-title', 'main > h1', 'main > h1[data-testid]', '#main h1[data-testid]', 'h1', 'h1:hover', 'h1:first-child', 'h1:not(.x)', '*', 'main *', 'html body main h1', 'body main > h1', 'main h1', '[data-page] h1', '[data-testid]', '[class]'. No match: '.page-title h1', '.panel h2', '.app-header h1', '.page-title-extra', 'h1 + p', 'h1 ~ p', 'h1::after', '.page-title::after', '[data-testid="nope"]', '[lang]', 'h1#main', 'h1[data-x="a b"]', 'main > h1[data-x]', '.checklist li:not(.x)'.

Run over 24 stylesheet mutations it reproduces the browser's verdict in every case: CLEAN on the shipped sheet, on '.page-title h1', on 'h1[data-x="a b"]', on '*', 'body', 'body !important' and on '.checklist li:not(.x)'; a named offender for '#main h1', '[data-testid="page-title"]', '[class~="page-title"]', a second '.page-title', 'h1[data-testid]', 'h1:hover', 'h1:first-child', 'main > h1[data-testid]', '#main h1[data-testid]', the '#main h1' form inside '@media (max-width: 900px)', the same rule declared above the class rule, '#main h1 { font: 700 2.4rem/1.6 system-ui }' and the comma list '#main h1, .panel h2'. The over-approximating direction creates no false-failure surface on the shipped stylesheet: over every selector in src/web/styles.css that declares font-size, line-height, margin, margin-top, margin-block or font, the new matcher reports '.page-title' and nothing else as reaching the page h1.

The element chain the matcher reasons about is read off the rendered markup, not assumed: html < body < main#main < h1.page-title, with attrs { class: 'page-title', 'data-testid': 'page-title' }. The h1's only emitter is layout() at src/web/pages.js:57, which every route goes through.

Issue #55's split: there is no split section, so no criterion is deferred or unanswered by this order.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep the existing text-matching resolver and extend mayReachPageTitle to also accept the attribute spellings — recognise '[class~="page-title"]' and '[data-testid="page-title"]' alongside '.page-title', fix the last-compound test to require the class to be on the h1, make the splitter bracket-aware, and add a winner-value cross-check.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is the same approach described more carefully, which is what a second attempt at this plan has to avoid. More decisively it leaves the defect in place: the guard would still be enumerating spellings rather than matching an element, so the next spelling QA does not think of — [class$="title"], [class^="page"], h1[class~=x] in a compound where the class is not the last simple selector, a renamed class in a compound like .panel.page-title — is another false pass. The over-approximating element match makes that whole class of shape unrepresentable rather than unwatched.

alternatives_considered.approach: Delete the cascade guard and replace it with a rule that the page h1's three properties are declared nowhere else in src/web/styles.css — grep the file for any other rule declaring font-size, line-height, margin or font and fail if one exists.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Too blunt in the other direction: '* { font-size: 2.4rem }' and 'body { font-size: 16px }' are in the shipped sheet and are both legitimate, so this would fail on a clean tree. It also cannot express '#main h1' inside a media query as an override rather than as noise, and it is the shape the project already rejected for #55 in attempt 1's own alternatives — the trade is precision for a false-failure surface on ordinary CSS.

alternatives_considered.approach: Model the page h1 as a fixed literal descriptor ({ tag: 'h1', class: 'page-title', id: null, parent: 'main#main' }) inside the guard rather than scanning the rendered HTML for it.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Cheaper by about fifteen lines, and it keeps the exact failure mode QA found: the guard's idea of the page h1 would again be a hand-written string that a markup change can move away from without the guard noticing. The scan is what makes the guard read the element the markup renders, and it is the same hook .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md already calls stable. A coordinated rename still has to be handled, but there the class is read off the resolved element rather than written down twice.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep the throw-on-unsupported contract and only widen the vocabulary enough to parse ':not(' and '+'/'~' correctly, so the guard can still refuse CSS it cannot model.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It keeps the failure that produced BUG-4 in spirit: the guard turns red on CSS that is merely unusual rather than on CSS that breaks the page title. With a one-directional match there is nothing left to refuse — anything undecidable resolves to 'may match', which is reported, and a report is already a red build with a message naming the selector. The throw only added a second, blunter way of going red, and on 'h1:hover' it would have failed the suite on CSS that cannot break anything.

alternatives_considered.approach: Add a headless-browser test that reads the computed font-size and margin-top of the rendered h1 in CI, so no model of CSS is needed at all.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Unchanged from attempt 1 and still refused by the same two facts: Playwright needs browser binaries on the clean CI runner, and jsdom computes no layout, so it returns no used values. conventions.md forbids a new runtime dependency by default. The project's existing answer is a browser acceptance criterion QA drives every run, which is what AC-1 is and what AC-7 to AC-11 make unmissable on the test side.

alternatives_considered.approach: Fix only the two false passes (BUG-1, BUG-2) and leave the two false alarms (BUG-3, BUG-4), on the grounds that they fail loudly rather than silently.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: BUG-3's message asserts as fact a change that does not occur, which sends the next developer hunting a rendering bug that is not there — and the guard is meant to be trusted precisely when it says the page title is wrong. More importantly the two are not separable: BUG-3's last-compound test and BUG-1's spelling whitelist are the same decision, made in two places with opposite errors. Fixing one without the other leaves a matcher that is neither sound nor complete, which is the state this ticket is in now.
